chapter.title: .NET Using ooRexx: the Rexx.Net API
chapter.para: A .NET program runs Rexx code through the assembly Rexx.Net.dll: it references the NuGet package Rexx.Net (dotnet add package Rexx.Net --prerelease), or the assembly of a build or of an installation. An installed ooRexx 5, 64-bit, is a prerequisite: the assembly finds librexx (rexx.dll on Windows) itself, through the rexx on the PATH or the system's places. Its public types are in the namespace Rexx.Net. This chapter describes the interpreter and the objects; , what the application gives the Rexx code (commands, streams, functions) and how it stops it. The signatures are C#'s; VB.NET, F# and PowerShell use the same types.

section.title: RexxInterpreter Class
section.para: An ooRexx interpreter instance. A process may have several, each with its own .local, packages and ADDRESS environments. It is IDisposable: Dispose ends the instance, on the thread that created it.

listitem.para: A new interpreter instance, with . The thread that calls it is attached to the instance until Dispose, which must run on that thread.
The instance whose Rexx code is calling .NET on this thread, or null (); and whether ooRexx made it (a program started by rexx) rather than Create. Dispose does nothing on an instance ooRexx made.
The interpreter's version ("5.3.0") and language level ("6.06").

Runs source (clauses separated by semicolons or line feeds) as a routine, with the arguments (USE ARG), and returns what it returns (RETURN): a RexxObject, or null for &nil; or no result; or converted to T (). The source may have directives (::requires, classes, routines) after its code.
Calls the Rexx program in the file path with the arguments, as CALL would, and returns its result.
A routine made from source under name, to call many times (): compiled once.
A package from a file, as ::requires loads one; or from source under name, which a later ::requires "name" of the instance's code finds ().
A class by name, as Rexx finds .Name (the environment, the instance's packages); null if there is none.

.environment and .local, as RexxObjects: rexx.Local["FORM"] = form makes .form the .NET object for the Rexx code. Pick names that are not Rexx classes': .list is Rexx's List class, whatever .local holds.

A new Rexx Array of the items, or a Directory or StringTable of the pairs, the values converted as arguments are: the explicit copies of .NET collections into Rexx ones (a .NET collection given to Rexx is a NetObject, by reference).

Keeps this thread attached to the instance until the RexxScope it returns is disposed: using (rexx.Enter()) { ... } for a batch of calls from a thread other than the creating one, or from .NET code that Rexx called (each call there attaches nested). Attaching costs about 20 µs, a message about 1 µs ().
Loads net.cls, so that Rexx code can use &net; without requiring it ().
The Rexx objects that .NET holds now, or that wait to be released: for diagnostics.

section.title: RexxOptions Class
section.para: The options of RexxInterpreter.Create: ooRexx's own instance options, and the bridge's.

listitem.para: The initial ADDRESS environment (an environment of the application, ).

Where external routines and ::requires files are looked for, and the extensions tried (".rex,.cls"). ooRexx's own folder of .cls files (where logicalwrapper.cls and json.cls are: that of rexx.dll, or the bin beside the lib of librexx) is always added at the end: ooRexx's rexx finds them through the PATH, which a .NET application need not have.
Native libraries loaded when the instance is created.
The Rexx code's standard streams, from the start ().

Whether Rexx code may use .NET from the start: by default, net.cls and CLR.CLS (built into the assembly) and the native library are registered with ooRexx when the instance is created, so ::requires "net.cls" needs no file (). false: only when a .NET object first goes to Rexx.
BSF4ooRexx's prefixes on the standard streams that the application has not taken ().

A token cancelled while a Run, Call or RunFile is starting halts the code at its first clause, instead of being missed (). It uses ooRexx's RXINI exit, which every program or routine call in the instance then goes through: about 0.3 µs more a call. false leaves it out, for code that calls routines in tight loops and is never cancelled.

section.title: RexxObject Class
section.para: Any Rexx object, by reference, as BSF4ooRexx's RexxProxy is in Java: it keeps the Rexx object alive while .NET holds it, and the same Rexx object is the same RexxObject each time (identity). It is a DynamicObject, so C#'s dynamic (and VB.NET's late binding) sends Rexx messages; and it is enumerable.

listitem.para: Sends the message name (uppercased, as Rexx does with every message) with the arguments: Rexx's o~name(args). The result as for Run. With a CancellationToken, the Rexx code is halted when it is cancelled ().

BSF4ooRexx's names for Send (and the Python bridge's): any string is a name, one held in a variable or one that is no C# name ("[]=", "||"). SendMessageScope starts the method search at the class scope, as Rexx's o~name:scope. As with any params method, an object[] given alone is the argument list; to send one Rexx Array, wrap it.
o[i] and o[i, j] = v: Rexx's own [] and []=, from 1 for an Array.
Whether the object is an instance of the class (or of a subclass), and whether it has a method of that name.
The object's o~supplier, as (index, item) pairs, taken now; foreach gives its items.
The object's o~string.
Releases the Rexx object now; else it is released after .NET collects the proxy. Optional.

section.para: Names are uppercased, so there is no case to guess. C#'s named arguments are not supported. In VB.NET, a Rexx object typed Object with Option Strict Off is late-bound the same way (a class's New is [New] there).

section.title: RexxString Class
section.para: A Rexx string, as a result: a RexxObject that holds the value, copied (no reference to keep). It compares by value (Rexx's strict ==: Equals, GetHashCode, C#'s ==), so it can be a dictionary key. Its value converts, explicitly or through dynamic implicitly, to string, every numeric type, bool and char, by Rexx's rules (" 1E3 " is 1000; only 1 and 0 are logical values); and its operators are Rexx's: "150" + 1 is 151. It implements IConvertible, with the type code String, for VB.NET and Convert.

section.title: RexxClass, RexxRoutine and RexxPackage Classes
section.para: Typed views of Rexx objects, as FindClass, Compile and LoadPackage return them.
A RexxRoutine is also callable through dynamic: dynamic twice = rexx.Compile(...); twice(21).

section.title: RexxConvert, RexxValue and RexxScope Classes
section.para: RexxConvert.To converts a Rexx result (a RexxString, a RexxObject, null) to a .NET type by Rexx's rules, as Run<T> does (); ToBool takes Rexx's logical values, "1" and "0". RexxValue.Omitted is an argument left out: rexx.Run(src, 1, RexxValue.Omitted, 3) makes arg(2, "O") true. A RexxScope is what Enter returns.

section.title: Values Between .NET and Rexx
section.para: .NET values given to Rexx (arguments, Local[...] =, the results of command handlers and functions) follow : strings and numbers as Rexx strings, bool as .LogicalWrapper~true or .LogicalWrapper~false (ooRexx's logicalwrapper.cls; one that comes back is a bool again: Run<object>, the arguments of functions), null as &nil;, a RexxObject as its Rexx object, RexxValue.Omitted as an omitted argument, and any other object (arrays and collections too) as a NetObject, by reference.

Rexx results are &nil; as null, a string as a RexxString, a NetObject as its .NET object where the result is typed object (dynamic, the indexer, foreach, Run<T>; where it is typed RexxObject, a proxy whose NetValue is the object), and any other object as a RexxObject. Where the result is converted to a type (Run<T>, Send<T>, Call<T>, RexxConvert.To), a string converts by Rexx's rules, a one-dimensional Rexx Array to a T[], a List<T> or an interface an array has, and a StringTable or a Directory to a dictionary with string keys: copies, their items converted. Anything that does not convert is an InvalidCastException.

section.title: RexxException Class
section.para: A Rexx condition, as a .NET exception: one that ends a call into Rexx (also a compile error), or one that a Rexx handler or override raised while .NET called it ().
Its Message is the secondary message, else the error text. A 98.900 that carried a .NET exception has it as its InnerException: the very object thrown.

section.title: Threads and Lifetime
section.para: Any .NET thread may call Rexx. A thread that runs no Rexx code is attached to the instance for the call and detached after it; a thread that is already inside Rexx (.NET code that Rexx called, a handler, a command handler) makes the call nested, on that thread: attached again, nested, so that a condition the Rexx code lets out stops there, as in any call (a HALT comes back as a HALT, ). One Rexx thread runs at a time in an instance (the interpreter's lock): .NET threads that call Rexx take turns, and Rexx's own concurrency (REPLY, start) interleaves with them as usual. using (rexx.Enter()) keeps a thread attached for a batch of calls. There is no asynchronous API: Rexx code is synchronous, and Task.Run(() => rexx.Run(...)) works because any thread can attach.

Lifetime. A RexxObject holds a global reference to its Rexx object, released by Dispose or, failing that, after .NET collects the proxy (its finalizer queues the release, done at the next call into the instance or when it ends). RexxStrings hold nothing. An instance's objects are released when it ends.

Not a sandbox. Rexx code can do what the process can: ADDRESS SYSTEM, files, &net;. An application that wants less sets InitialAddress to an environment of its own and Net to false; even so, the interpreter is no security boundary.
